usamts-2014-r3-01.title: Start from the forced runs
usamts-2014-r3-01.body:
A run of unshaded cells is determined by its first term and common difference, so start where two entries of one run are given.

* **Bottom row, left run.** The run in columns 1–6 contains $31, 26$ in columns 5–6, so its difference is $-5$: $51, 46, 41, 36, 31, 26$.
* **Left part.** Let $t$ be the entry in row 3, column 1. Column 1 (rows 3–5) is $t, \frac{t + 51}{2}, 51$, so $t$ is odd. Row 3 (columns 1–4) is $t, 10, 20 - t, 30 - 2t$. Column 4 (all five rows, ending in 36) has $30 - 2t$ in row 3, so its difference is $t + 3$ and its top entry is $24 - 4t > 0$, so $t \le 5$. Row 1 (columns 1–6) starts with 3 and has $24 - 4t$ in column 4, so $3 \mid 21 - 4t$, i.e. $3 \mid t$. Hence $t = 3$: row 3 is $3, 10, 17, 24$, column 1 is $3, 27, 51$, column 4 is $12, 18, 24, 30, 36$, and row 1 is $3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18$. Column 6 runs from 18 to 26: $18, 20, 22, 24, 26$. Column 3 (rows 1–3) is $9, 13, 17$, so row 2 (columns 3–4) is $13, 18$ ✓.
* **Right part.** Let $h$ be the difference of column 8 ($59, 59 + h, \dots, 59 + 4h$). Row 2 (columns 6–9) starts at 20 and has $59 + h$ in column 8, so $h$ is odd; the bottom-right run goes from $59 + 4h$ to 59 in three steps, so $3 \mid h$. Then row 1 (from 59), column 9 (rows 1–3), row 3 (columns 8–11) and column 11 (rows 3–5, ending in 59) must all stay between 1 and 99. Checking the few remaining cases leaves only $h = -9$, with row 2 difference 15 and row 1 difference 12. This gives row 2 $= 20, 35, 50, 65$, column 8 $= 59, 50, 41, 32, 23$, row 1 right $= 59, 71, 83, 95$, row 3 right $= 41, 59, 77, 95$, bottom-right $= 23, 35, 47, 59$, and column 11 (rows 3–5) $= 95, 77, 59$.

The completed grid:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 3 & 6 & 9 & 12 & 15 & 18 & \blacksquare & 59 & 71 & 83 & 95\\\hline \blacksquare & \blacksquare & 13 & 18 & \blacksquare & 20 & 35 & 50 & 65 & \blacksquare & \blacksquare\\\hline 3 & 10 & 17 & 24 & \blacksquare & 22 & \blacksquare & 41 & 59 & 77 & 95\\\hline 27 & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & 30 & \blacksquare & 24 & \blacksquare & 32 & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & 77\\\hline 51 & 46 & 41 & 36 & 31 & 26 & \blacksquare & 23 & 35 & 47 & 59\\\hline\end{array}$$
($\blacksquare$ = shaded cell)

**Check.** Every maximal run of unshaded cells is arithmetic: for example column 8 is $59, 50, 41, 32, 23$ (difference $-9$) and column 9 is $71, 65, 59$; all entries are positive and less than 100.

usamts-2014-r3-02.title: Compare congruent triangles
usamts-2014-r3-02.body:
The 10-sided polygon is the pentagon plus five "tip" triangles, one on each side. Each tip triangle has base 1 and base angles equal to the exterior angle of the pentagon, $72^\circ$; call its area $T$.

Cut the pentagon along the diagonals $A_2A_5$ and $A_3A_5$ into:
* the triangle $A_5A_1A_2$, area $y$ (two sides 1 with a $108^\circ$ angle);
* the triangle $A_3A_4A_5$, also area $y$ (congruent to the first);
* the triangle $A_2A_3A_5$, area $z$.

**Shaded part:** trapezoid $A_2A_3A_4A_5$ plus the tips on $A_2A_3$ and $A_4A_5$ (points $B_5$, $B_2$ lie on line $A_3A_4$), area $y + z + 2T$.

**Unshaded part:** triangle $A_5A_1A_2$ plus the other three tips, area $y + 3T$.

Now $\angle A_4A_3A_5 = \frac12(180^\circ - 108^\circ) = 36^\circ$, so $\angle A_2A_3A_5 = 108^\circ - 36^\circ = 72^\circ$, and likewise at $A_2$. So triangle $A_2A_3A_5$ is isosceles with base $A_2A_3 = 1$ and base angles $72^\circ$, the same as the tip triangle on $A_2A_3$. Two triangles on the same base with the same base angles are congruent: $z = T$.

Hence shaded $= y + 3T =$ unshaded, and the ratio is $\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

usamts-2014-r3-02.title: Coordinates check
usamts-2014-r3-02.body:
Place the pentagon with circumradius 1 and $A_1$ at the bottom. The tips $B_5$ and $B_2$ lie on line $A_3A_4$ at height $\cos 36^\circ$, and computing the two areas with the shoelace formula (for example numerically) gives
$$\frac{[A_2A_5B_2B_5]}{[\text{star}]} = 0.5000\ldots,$$
in agreement with the exact answer $\frac12$ found above (the ratio does not depend on the size of the pentagon).

usamts-2014-r3-03.title: Monotone and multiplicative means a power
usamts-2014-r3-03.body:
**The sequence is non-decreasing.** From (i), $a_{n^k} = a_n^k$. For any $n$ and $k$, $n^k < (n+1)^k$, so by (ii)
$$a_n^k = a_{n^k} < Ba_{(n+1)^k} = Ba_{n+1}^k,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad\left(\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}\right)^k < B$$
for every $k$; hence $a_n \le a_{n+1}$. Also (i) with $m = 1$ gives $a_1 = 1$.

**Case $a_2 = 1$.** Then $a_{2^k} = 1$ for all $k$, and monotonicity squeezes every $a_n$ between $a_1 = 1$ and $a_{2^k} = 1$, so $a_n = 1$ and both logarithms are 0.

**Case $a_2 = \lambda > 1$.** Fix $n \ge 2$ (so $a_n \ge a_2 > 1$). For large $p$ choose $q$ with $n^q < 2^p \le n^{q+1}$. Monotonicity gives $a_n^q \le \lambda^p \le a_n^{q+1}$. Taking $\log_2$:
$$q\log_2 n < p \le (q+1)\log_2 n,\qquad q\log_2 a_n \le p\log_2\lambda \le (q+1)\log_2 a_n.$$
Dividing (all quantities positive),
$$\frac{q}{q+1}\log_n a_n \le \log_2\lambda \le \frac{q+1}{q}\log_n a_n.$$
As $p \to \infty$, $q \to \infty$, so $\log_n a_n = \log_2\lambda$ for every $n \ge 2$ (i.e. $a_n = n^c$ with $c = \log_2\lambda$).

In both cases $\log_{2015}a_{2015} = \log_{2014}a_{2014}$, so the difference is 0 (and the value 0 does occur, e.g. for $a_n = n$).

**Answer: 0**

usamts-2014-r3-04.title: A prime witness for each adjacent pair
usamts-2014-r3-04.body:
Write $\nu_p(m)$ for the exponent of the prime $p$ in $m$. Let the numbers be $x_1, \dots, x_9$ around the circle (indices mod 9). For each $i$, $n \nmid x_ix_{i+1}$, so there is a prime $p_i$ with
$$\nu_{p_i}(x_i) + \nu_{p_i}(x_{i+1}) < \nu_{p_i}(n).$$

**No prime witnesses two non-consecutive pairs.** Suppose $p = p_i = p_j$ where the pairs $\{x_i, x_{i+1}\}$ and $\{x_j, x_{j+1}\}$ are disjoint, and let $k = \nu_p(n)$. Adding the two witness inequalities: $\nu_p(x_i) + \nu_p(x_{i+1}) + \nu_p(x_j) + \nu_p(x_{j+1}) < 2k$. But $x_i, x_j$ are non-adjacent and so are $x_{i+1}, x_{j+1}$ (in a 9-cycle with disjoint, non-consecutive pairs), so $\nu_p(x_i) + \nu_p(x_j) \ge k$ and $\nu_p(x_{i+1}) + \nu_p(x_{j+1}) \ge k$ — contradiction.

So each prime is a witness for at most two pairs, and then they are consecutive pairs $i, i+1$ (three pairs would include two disjoint ones).

**A prime used twice divides $n$ squared.** If $p = p_i = p_{i+1}$ and $\nu_p(n) = 1$, then none of $x_i, x_{i+1}, x_{i+2}$ is divisible by $p$; but $x_i, x_{i+2}$ are non-adjacent, so $p \mid n \mid x_ix_{i+2}$ — contradiction. So $p^2 \mid n$.

**Lower bound.** Every witness divides $n$, and the nine pairs use primes with multiplicity at most 2, each prime used twice dividing $n$ to at least the second power. So $n$ is divisible by a product of nine primes, each appearing at most twice. The smallest such product takes the nine smallest entries of $2, 2, 3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 11, 11, \dots$:
$$n \ge 2^2\cdot3^2\cdot5^2\cdot7^2\cdot11 = 485100.$$

**Construction.** With $n = 485100$ take, in order around the circle,
$$\frac{n}{2\cdot11},\ \frac{n}{2^2},\ \frac{n}{2\cdot3},\ \frac{n}{3^2},\ \frac{n}{3\cdot5},\ \frac{n}{5^2},\ \frac{n}{5\cdot7},\ \frac{n}{7^2},\ \frac{n}{7\cdot11}.$$
The product of two of these is $n^2$ divided by the product of their two denominators. For adjacent numbers the denominators share a prime $p$ whose total exponent exceeds $\nu_p(n)$ (e.g. $2\cdot11$ and $2^2$ give $2^3 > 2^2$), so the product is not a multiple of $n$. For non-adjacent numbers the denominators multiply to a divisor of $n$, so the product is a multiple of $n$. The nine numbers are distinct.

**Answer: 485100** ($= 2^2\cdot3^2\cdot5^2\cdot7^2\cdot11$)

usamts-2014-r3-05.title: Laser loops
usamts-2014-r3-05.body:
Each triangle has legs $\sqrt2$ and area 1, so the number of triangles equals the number of unit squares in $S$. Each triangle consists of two half-squares (cut by a diagonal), each having its right angle at the midpoint $M$ of the triangle's hypotenuse, which is a grid point.

**The laser.** Treat every hypotenuse as a two-sided mirror and every leg as glass. Start a laser at the midpoint $M$ of some hypotenuse, heading into one half of its triangle along the diagonal of that unit square perpendicular to the cut. It crosses the square through its centre and arrives at the opposite corner of the square. The other half of this square belongs to a tile whose hypotenuse midpoint is exactly that corner, so the laser hits that tile's mirror at $45^\circ$, reflects, and crosses the next square. So the laser moves from square to square, crossing each visited square along a diagonal.

Since there are finitely many squares and the motion is reversible, the path is a closed loop, and it never crosses a square twice: crossing a square in the opposite direction would force the loop to be its own reverse, which needs a perpendicular reflection, and that never happens. Each tile it meets is crossed in both of its halves (in through one, reflect, out through the other), so the loop consists of whole squares and whole tiles.

**Counting.** Let $a, b, c, d$ be the numbers of squares crossed going NW, NE, SW, SE. Each crossing moves the laser one unit vertically and one unit horizontally, and the loop closes up:
* north = south: $a + b = c + d$;
* west = east: $a + c = b + d$;
* a reflection in a horizontal or vertical mirror turns NW/SE travel into NE/SW travel and vice versa, so the two kinds alternate: $a + d = b + c$.

Adding the first two equations gives $a = d$; the first and third give $a = c$; the last two give $a = b$. So the loop crosses $4a$ squares, i.e. it uses $4a$ whole tiles.

**Finish.** Remove the tiles of this loop. What remains is again a set of squares tiled according to the rules, so we repeat. Each loop removes a multiple of 4 tiles, so the total number of triangles is a multiple of 4. ∎
